title: In the Matter of Request for Opinion of the Justices
description: Whether the method of arriving at a plurality of votes cast through the use of ranked-choice voting, as amended by L.D. 1666, conforms with the provisions of the Maine Constitution requiring election by a plurality of votes for Governor, State Senator, and State Representative.
plaintiff_argument: Proponents of L.D. 1666 argue that the Constitution's plurality requirement does not constrain the Legislature from determining how that plurality is achieved, and ranked-choice voting is a valid method that comports with the Maine Constitution.
defendant_argument: Opponents of L.D. 1666 argue that the legislation would violate the Maine Constitution because the Constitution defines a 'vote' as a single choice counted in one round, and ranked-choice voting's multi-round tabulation is inconsistent with this definition.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that L.D. 1666, if enacted, would violate the Maine Constitution's provisions for the election of State Representatives, State Senators, and the Governor by a plurality of all votes.

title: State v. Engroff
description: Whether Aaron C. Engroff's speedy trial rights were violated and whether the admission of a video interview of the victim violated his confrontation and due process rights, with Engroff arguing for violation and the State arguing against it.
plaintiff_argument: Engroff argued that his speedy trial right was violated due to excessive delay and that the admission of the victim's video interview violated his rights under the Maine Confrontation Clause and Maine Due Process Clause, asserting the statute authorizing the video's admission did not apply to his case.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Engroff's speedy trial right was not violated, that the admission of the video interview did not violate the Maine Confrontation Clause or Due Process Clause, and that the statute authorizing the video's admission applied to his case.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of conviction, finding no speedy trial violation and no violation of confrontation or due process rights regarding the video's admission, citing a subsequent statutory amendment that clarified the statute's applicability.

title: Maine State Chamber of Commerce v. Department of Labor
description: Whether the Maine Department of Labor's rules for the Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) program, specifically regarding nonrefundable premiums and the delay in applying for private substitute plans, are legal and constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Department's rules conflict with the PFML Act, are arbitrary and capricious, and constitute an unconstitutional taking of private property without just compensation under both the Maine and U.S. Constitutions.
defendant_argument: The Department argued that its rules are consistent with the PFML Act, are a reasonable implementation to ensure a fiscally sound fund, and do not constitute an unconstitutional taking because participation is voluntary and no identifiable property right is at stake.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Department of Labor's rules for the Paid Family and Medical Leave program are legal and constitutional, finding they do not conflict with the Act, are not arbitrary or capricious, and do not constitute an unconstitutional taking of private property.

title: State v. McLain
description: Whether Derric McLain validly waived his constitutional privilege against self-incrimination under the Maine Constitution during custodial interrogation.
plaintiff_argument: McLain argued that he did not waive his privilege against self-incrimination and ambiguously invoked his right to counsel, requiring law enforcement to cease questioning or clarify his intent.
defendant_argument: The State argued that McLain had waived his privilege against self-incrimination.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the judgment of conviction and remanded for further proceedings, ruling that McLain's custodial statements must be suppressed because he did not clearly waive his right against self-incrimination.

title: Dupuis v. Roman Catholic Bishop of Portland
description: Whether the retroactive application of 14 M.R.S. § 752-C(3), which revives previously time-barred claims for child sexual abuse, violates the Maine Constitution by infringing upon a constitutionally protected vested right to be free from suit.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that 14 M.R.S. § 752-C(3) is a constitutional legislative response to address the unique circumstances of delayed disclosure by child sexual abuse victims, allowing them to pursue justice for their injuries.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the retroactive application of 14 M.R.S. § 752-C(3) is unconstitutional because the expiration of a statute of limitations creates a vested right to be free from suit, which cannot be retroactively impaired by legislation.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the retroactive application of 14 M.R.S. § 752-C(3) is unconstitutional as applied to expired claims, thereby upholding the defendant's statute of limitations defense.

title: Parker v. Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
description: Whether Maine's longstanding Sunday hunting ban conflicts with the recently enacted right-to-food amendment to the Maine Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Sunday hunting ban has been rendered unconstitutional by the right-to-food amendment, which enshrines a right to harvest food through hunting.
defendant_argument: The Sunday hunting ban does not conflict with the right-to-food amendment because hunting in violation of the ban is illegal, and the right to hunt created by the amendment does not extend to illegal hunting.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the dismissal of the complaint and declared that Maine's longstanding Sunday hunting ban is constitutional and does not conflict with the right-to-food amendment.

title: In re Opinion of the Justices
description: Whether the Governor's role impacts the direct initiation of legislation under the Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor concurs with arguments in the Attorney General's brief regarding the Governor's role in the direct initiation of legislation.
defendant_argument: The document does not present an opposing argument, as it is a submission from the Governor to the court.
decision_outcome: The court's decision is not provided in this document, as it is a submission to the court.

title: Winchester v. State
description: Whether counsel's failure to assert Dennis F. Winchester's right to a speedy trial constituted ineffective assistance of counsel, entitling him to dismissal of charges, with the plaintiff arguing it did and the defendant arguing it did not.
plaintiff_argument: Winchester argues that his counsel's failures to assert his right to a speedy trial constituted ineffective assistance of counsel, which prejudiced his ability to obtain dismissal of charges.
defendant_argument: The State, by defending the PCR court's denial of Winchester's petitions, implicitly argues that Winchester's speedy trial rights were not violated and his counsel was not ineffective.
decision_outcome: The judgment of the post-conviction review court, which denied Winchester's petitions, is vacated, and the case is remanded for reconsideration consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

title: Black v. Bureau of Parks & Lands
description: Whether the Bureau of Parks and Lands had the constitutional and statutory authority to lease public reserved land for a transmission line without a formal administrative process and legislative approval, and whether a citizen's initiative could retroactively invalidate such a lease.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Bureau's lease of public reserved land for a transmission line was ultra vires because it substantially altered the land, requiring a two-thirds legislative vote, and that the Bureau failed to follow a required public administrative process. They also contended that a citizen's initiative retroactively invalidated the lease.
defendant_argument: The defendants (Bureau and CMP) argued that the Bureau had broad statutory authority to grant such leases without a formal administrative process or legislative approval, as the lease did not "substantially alter" the land. They also argued that the citizen's initiative could not constitutionally apply retroactively to invalidate the existing lease.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the lower court's judgment and remanded for entry of judgment in favor of the Bureau of Parks and Lands, NECEC Transmission LLC, and Central Maine Power Co. on all counts of the first amended complaint.

title: State v. White
description: Whether the trial court erred in denying the defendant's repeated motions for a mistrial due to prosecutorial errors, specifically improper comments during opening and closing arguments, and whether these errors, especially in the context of racial bias, warrant a new trial.
plaintiff_argument: White argues that the trial court erred in denying his motions for a mistrial based on improper prosecutorial comments, including urging the jury to find him guilty, referencing his decision not to testify, and implicitly invoking racial bias, which collectively warranted a new trial.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the prosecutor's comments were not error or were remedied by curative instructions, and that the overwhelming evidence of guilt meant any errors were harmless and did not warrant a new trial.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Maine vacated the judgment of conviction and remanded the case for a new trial, finding that prosecutorial errors impaired the defendant's substantial rights.

title: NECEC Transmission LLC v. Bureau of Parks & Lands
description: Whether retroactively applying sections 4 and 5 of the Initiative to the certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) issued for the Project, as required by section 6, violates the due process clause of the Maine Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: NECEC argues that the retroactive application of the Initiative to its CPCN is unconstitutional as it deprives them of vested rights under the Maine Constitution's due process clause.
defendant_argument: The State argues that the vested rights doctrine is common law and can be abrogated by citizen-initiated legislation, and that the Initiative does not violate due process.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that section 6 of the Initiative, which mandates retroactive application of sections 4 and 5 to the CPCN, is unconstitutional if NECEC can prove it acquired vested rights through substantial good-faith construction.

title: State v. Reeves
description: Whether the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to dismiss based on the Interstate Compact on Detainers, whether the hallway bench conferences violated his public trial rights, and whether denying his mid-trial request to represent himself violated his constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the trial court correctly denied Reeves's motion to dismiss because the 120-day deadline was tolled due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and that Reeves's other arguments regarding public trial rights and self-representation were without merit or unpreserved.
defendant_argument: Reeves argued that the State failed to comply with the Interstate Compact on Detainers by not bringing him to trial within 120 days, that holding bench conferences in the hallway violated his public trial rights, and that denying his mid-trial request to represent himself violated his constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Judicial Court of Maine affirmed the judgment of the trial court, upholding Carine Reeves's conviction for intentional or knowing murder.

title: Portland Regional Chamber of Commerce v. City of Portland
description: Whether voter-initiated legislation establishing an emergency minimum wage in Portland is valid under the Maine Constitution and Portland City Code, and if so, what its effective date is.
plaintiff_argument: The emergency minimum wage provision was not validly enacted and, if valid, should not take effect until January 1, 2022.
defendant_argument: The emergency minimum wage provision was validly enacted and its effective date is January 1, 2022.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Superior Court's judgment, ruling that the voter-initiated emergency minimum wage provision is valid and becomes effective on January 1, 2022.
